figures.title: The Additive Family Tree
figures.subtitle: Additives grouped by the job they do.

segments.name: Additives
segments.text: Module three is about additives: substances added to food on purpose to do a job. This tree sorts them by that job.

segments.name: Four Jobs
segments.text: There are four main jobs. Appearance, which means colors. Shelf life: preservatives and antioxidants. Texture: thickeners, emulsifiers and anti-caking agents. And taste: acids, flavor enhancers and sweeteners.
segments.cue: The second and third rows, left to right

segments.name: One Example Each
segments.text: The bottom row gives one example of each, with its E-number, from curcumin, E100, to aspartame, E951. Each box links to its figure.

segments.name: E for Europe
segments.text: An E-number is the code an additive gets once it passes a European safety review. The hundreds digit roughly tells you the job: one for colors, two for preservatives, three for antioxidants and acids, four for thickeners and emulsifiers, five for acidity regulators and anti-caking agents, six for flavor enhancers, and nine for sweeteners and glazes.

segments.name: Not All Synthetic
segments.text: There are exceptions, which is why we group by job. And many additives are ordinary food compounds: vitamin C is E300, and pectin from apples is E440.

figures.title: What Counts as an Additive
figures.subtitle: Definition, labels and approval, with citric acid as the first example.

segments.name: Added on Purpose
segments.text: An additive is added to do a technical job: to color, preserve, thicken, sweeten or stop clumping. Ordinary ingredients like flour, salt and sugar aren't usually called additives.

segments.name: Same Molecule
segments.text: Ingredients are listed by weight, so additives are usually near the end. And an additive is the same molecule whether it came from a fruit or a factory; what matters is the amount, and the food it's in.

segments.name: Citric Acid
segments.text: Our first example is citric acid, E330. Three acid groups give the sour taste of lemons and limes, around a central carbon with an OH.

segments.name: In You and in Lemons
segments.text: Your own cells make citric acid every day: it starts the citric acid cycle that releases energy from food. Most added citric acid is made by fermenting sugar with a mold.

segments.name: Rules and Labels
segments.text: In the US, the FDA approves additives, or they're generally recognized as safe, and labels list them by name. In the EU, labels give the job plus the name or E-number. Worldwide, the INS number is the same digits without the E.

figures.title: Colors
figures.subtitle: From turmeric to azo dyes and titanium dioxide.

segments.name: Curcumin
segments.text: Curcumin, E100, is the yellow of turmeric. Two rings are joined by a long chain of alternating single and double bonds. That chain absorbs blue light, so it looks yellow.

segments.name: Plant Colors
segments.text: Other colors from whole foods include beet red, paprika and beta-carotene.

segments.name: Red 40
segments.text: Allura Red, also called Red 40 or E129, is a synthetic dye made from petroleum. An N=N azo bond joins two ring systems, and charged sulfonate groups make it dissolve in water.

segments.name: Warnings and Phase-Outs
segments.text: In the EU, foods with Red 40 or five other synthetic colors must carry a warning about activity and attention in children. In 2025 the FDA said it plans to phase out petroleum-based dyes.

segments.name: Titanium Dioxide
segments.text: Titanium dioxide, E171, is a white mineral pigment. The EU banned it as a food additive from 2022, because harm to DNA couldn't be ruled out. The US still allows it, up to one percent of a food's weight.

segments.name: Sorbic and Benzoic Acid
segments.text: The most common preservatives against molds and yeasts are sorbic acid, E200, and benzoic acid, E210, often used as their salts, potassium sorbate and sodium benzoate. In acidic foods they slip into microbe cells and stop them growing.

segments.name: From Berries
segments.text: Sorbic acid was first found in rowan berries, and benzoic acid occurs naturally in cranberries and cinnamon. With vitamin C, heat and light, benzoate can form traces of benzene, so many drinks were reformulated.

segments.name: Nitrite
segments.text: Nitrite, a nitrogen with two oxygens, cures bacon, ham and salami. Sodium nitrite is E250. It stops the bacterium that causes botulism, and gives cured meat its pink color and flavor.

segments.name: Nitrosamines
segments.text: At high heat, nitrite can form nitrosamines, which we'll meet in Processing. Most nitrate in the diet actually comes from vegetables, and meats labeled uncured are usually cured with celery powder.

segments.name: Sulfites
segments.text: Sulfur dioxide and sulfites, E220 to E228, preserve wine and dried fruit. They can trigger asthma in sensitive people, so US labels must declare them, and they destroy thiamin.

figures.title: Antioxidants and Acids
figures.subtitle: Stopping browning and rancidity, and adding tang.

segments.name: Vitamin C
segments.text: Vitamin C, E300, is the most familiar antioxidant additive. The two OH groups on the double bond give up electrons, so vitamin C is oxidized first and the food is protected from browning.

segments.name: BHA and BHT
segments.text: BHA and BHT, E320 and E321, are synthetic antioxidants. An OH on a ring gives up a hydrogen to stop the chain reaction that turns fat rancid, and bulky groups keep what's left stable.

segments.name: A Caution
segments.text: They're permitted in small amounts. The US National Toxicology Program lists BHA as reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen, based on high doses in animals.

segments.name: Phosphoric Acid
segments.text: Phosphoric acid, E338, gives colas their tang. Phosphate additives are absorbed more completely than phosphorus in whole foods, which matters in kidney disease. Vinegar, yogurt and apples supply other food acids.

figures.title: Thickeners and Emulsifiers
figures.subtitle: Gels, gums and molecules with two ends.

segments.name: Pectin
segments.text: Pectin, E440, is long chains of galacturonic acid: a sugar ring with an acid group. The chains trap water and, with sugar and acid, set jam. It's a soluble fiber from apples and citrus peel.

segments.name: Gums
segments.text: Most other thickeners come from plants too: agar and carrageenan from red seaweed, locust bean gum from carob, guar gum from guar beans. Xanthan gum is made by bacteria.

segments.name: Two Ends
segments.text: Emulsifiers keep oil and water mixed. This monoglyceride has a water-loving head, glycerol with two free OH groups, and a fat-loving tail, one fatty acid instead of a fat's three.

segments.name: Lecithin
segments.text: Mono- and diglycerides, E471, keep bread soft. Lecithin, E322, works the same way; egg yolk lecithin holds mayonnaise together.

segments.name: Gut Bacteria
segments.text: Early research in mice suggests some emulsifiers may disturb gut bacteria; evidence in people is still limited.

segments.name: Baking Soda
segments.text: Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, E500. With an acid it gives off carbon dioxide, which makes batter rise. Your pancreas releases bicarbonate too, to neutralize stomach acid.

segments.name: Anti-Caking
segments.text: Silica, E551, and calcium silicate soak up moisture so salt and spice mixes don't clump.

segments.name: MSG
segments.text: Monosodium glutamate, E621, is the amino acid glutamic acid with one acid group charged. In water it splits into glutamate and a sodium ion. Glutamate tastes savory, or umami.

segments.name: Same as in Tomatoes
segments.text: Your body handles glutamate from MSG the same way as glutamate from tomatoes, parmesan, mushrooms or kombu. Blinded studies haven't consistently reproduced the symptoms some people report, and MSG has about a third of the sodium of salt.

figures.title: Sweeteners
figures.subtitle: Intense sweeteners, sugar alcohols and the ADI.

segments.name: Aspartame
segments.text: Aspartame, E951, is two amino acids, aspartic acid and phenylalanine, with a methyl cap. It's about two hundred times sweeter than sugar.

segments.name: PKU and Safety
segments.text: People with PKU can't break down phenylalanine, so labels warn them. In 2023 the WHO's cancer agency classed aspartame as possibly carcinogenic, its lowest level, while WHO's expert committee kept the acceptable daily intake at forty milligrams per kilogram.

segments.name: Sucralose
segments.text: Compare sucrose, table sugar, with sucralose, E955. Three OH groups are swapped for chlorine. The result is about six hundred times sweeter and mostly isn't absorbed.

segments.name: Erythritol
segments.text: Erythritol is a sugar alcohol: a short chain with an OH on every carbon. It's about two-thirds as sweet as sugar with almost no calories. Other sugar alcohols cause gas in large amounts, and xylitol is poisonous to dogs.

segments.name: The ADI
segments.text: The acceptable daily intake is the amount per kilogram that can be eaten every day for life without appreciable risk, usually a hundredth of the highest harmless dose in animals.

figures.title: Putting It All Together
figures.subtitle: The whole lesson in one table, plus a few extras.

segments.name: One Table
segments.text: Here are the E-number ranges in one table: each range's main job, examples, and whole foods that contain the same or similar compounds.

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few extras. An E-number is an approval, not a warning. Uncured meat is still cured, with celery powder. And additives cluster in ultra-processed foods; whole foods need almost none. Try the quiz below.
